'''''Ranunculus baudotii''''', '''brackish water-crowfoot''', is a [[flowering plant]] in the [[Ranunculaceae]] (buttercup family). As the name suggests, it tends to grow near the sea, typically in pools and ditches in coastal marshes that are slightly salty due to sea spray. It can also be found inland where there is some saline influence. It is not edible and has economic uses, but it is generally valued as a plant of conservation interest and an indicator of less agriculturally improved habitat.

==Description==
Brackish water-crowfoot is an annual or [[perennial]] aquatic plant with stems up to 3 m (9 ft) long, becoming terrestrial as its habitat dries out in summer. The submerged capillary leaves are usually about 5 cm long, but exceptionally as much as 15 cm and are characteristically shorter than the adjacent stem [[Plant stem|internode]]. The floating and terrestrial laminar leaves are typically deeply 3-lobed (divided more than halfway to the base) with and up to 1 cm long by 2.5 cm wide. All the leaves are arranged alternately along the stem, with petioles up to about 8 cm long (or even 20 cm long in the case of some submerged leaves). At the base of each petiole is a small, ovate [[stipule]].
[[File:Ranunculus baudotii leaves.jpg|thumb|Plants characteristically have both laminar and capillary leaves.]]

Flowering occurs between May and September in Northern Europe. The flowers are borne singly on long [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicels]] arising opposite to a leaf (the pedicels are up to 10x as long as the corresponding petiole). The 5 petals are white with a yellow base, a lunate nectar pit, and are contiguous at [[anthesis]]. Each petal is about 1 cm long. There are also 5 [[Sepal|sepals]] about half as long as the petals, which are greenish with dark markings, especially at the tip. The [[Hermaphrodite|hermaphroditic]] flowers have 15–30 stamens and up to about 65 carpels.
[[File:Ranunculus baudotii 3.jpg|thumb|Close-up of the flower]]

The fruits are [[Achene|achenes]] 1.2–1.8 mm long with thin ventral and dorsal wings at maturity and a short, lateral beak.<ref name=Sell1>{{cite book |last1=Sell |first1=Peter |last2=Murrell |first2=Gina |title=Flora of Great Britain and Ireland, vol. 1 |date=2018 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge|isbn=978-0-521-55335-3}}</ref><ref name=Schou>{{Cite book |last1=Schou |first1=J.C. |last2=Moeslund |first2=B. |last3=van de Weyer |first3=K. |last4=Lansdown |first4=R.V. |last5=Wiegleb |first5=G. |last6=Holm |first6=P. |last7=Baastrup-Spohr |first7=L. |last8=Sand-Jensen |first8=K. |display-authors=1 |title=Aquatic Plants of Northern and Central Europe including Britain and Ireland |publisher=Princeton University Press |year=2023 |isbn=978-0-691-25101-1 |location=Princeton, N.J.}}</ref>

==Identification==
It can be very difficult to identify water-crowfoots. This species is distinguished by its habitat, which is usually very coastal, the combination of laminar and capillary leaves, and by the distinctive blue tips to the typically downward-pointing sepals.<ref name=Stace>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |date=2019 |location=Suffolk |publisher=C&M Floristics |edition=4th |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref> Confirmation requires examination of the winged achenes and the receptacle elongating in fruit.<ref>{{Cite web |title=PlantAtlas |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.5w6 |access-date=2024-03-09 |website=plantatlas2020.org}}</ref>

[[File:Ranunculus_baudotii_blue_tips.jpg|thumb|The sepals are recurved and blue-tipped.]]

==Taxonomy==
This species was overlooked until 1839, when the name ''Ranunculus baudotii'' was published by [[Dominique Alexandre Godron]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Godron, Dominique Alexandre (1807-1880) |url=https://www.ipni.org/a/3218-1 |access-date=1 March 2024 |website=International Plant Names Index}}</ref> in a journal in the French city of [[Nancy, France|Nancy]], giving the name in honour of the botanist Charles Joseph Auguste de Baudot, from nearby [[Sarrebourg]]. He was only just in time: in 1843 other names were independently given to similar plants in two publications in Scandinavia. It has accumulated many more synonyms since then: 35 of them are listed by the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew.<ref name=POWO>{{Cite web |title=Ranunculus baudotii Godr. |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:712287-1 |access-date=1 March 2024 |website=Plants of the World Online}}</ref> The most likely one to be encountered is ''Ranunculus peltatus'' subsp. ''baudotii'' <small>(Godr.) Meikle ex C.D.K. Cook</small>, which was coined in 1983 and has been used until recently in many botanical books.

It lies within the taxonomically difficult section Batrachium of the [[Ranunculaceae]], a family that is known to be [[Polyphyly|polyphyletic]] and therefore might be split. Some authors use the name ''Batrachium baudotii'' <small>(Godr.) F.W. Schultz</small>, which was originally coined in 1844 but may eventually be revived.<ref name="spalek" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Koutecký |first1=Petr |last2=Prančl |first2=Jan |last3=Košnar |first3=Jiří |date=2021 |title=Waking up from a taxonomist's nightmare: emerging structure of ''Ranunculus'' section Batrachium (Ranunculaceae) in central Europe based on molecular data and genome sizes |journal=Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society |volume=198 |issue=4 |pages=417–437 |doi=10.1093/botlinnean/boab063}}</ref>

Godron's type specimen is located at the Institut de Botanique of the Université de Montpellier (MPU).<ref name="gbif"/>

Brackish water-crowfoot is tetraploid (2n = 32) in the northern part of its range and diploid (2n = 16) in the south. The diploid populations are more similar to [[Ranunculus peltatus|pond water-crowfoot]] in appearance.<ref name="Schou" />

It is known to hybridise with ''[[Ranunculus trichophyllus]]'' to give ''R. x segretii'' <small> A. Félix</small> and with ''[[Ranunculus aquatilis|R. aquatilis]]'' to give ''R. x lambertii'' <small>A. Félix</small>. Both of these hybrids are sterile. A third hybrid with ''[[Ranunculus peltatus|R. peltatus]]'' has been artificially synthesised, but not yet found in the wild.<ref name=hybrids>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |last2=Preston |first2=C.D. |last3=Pearman |first3=D.A. |title=Hybrid Flora of the British Isles |date=2015 |publisher=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland |location=Bristol |isbn=978-0-901158-48-2}}</ref>

==Habitat and ecology==
This species grows mainly in coastal grasslands, where it occurs in slightly brackish seasonal pools. It can also be found in highly alkaline fens and even freshwater rivers and pools inland.<ref name="Schou" />
[[File:Ranunculus baudotii habitat.jpg|thumb|The habitat for brackish water-crowfoot is typically bare mud in drying pools.]]

Although it is normally found in coastal locations, below 10 m, it also occurs in [[Karst spring|karst springs]] in central Europe<ref name=spalek>{{Cite journal |last1=Spałek |first1=K. |last2=Prockow |first2=J. |date=2011 |title=Karst springs as habitats for rare and protected plant species: a new inland locality of a halophyte plant ''Batrachium baudotii'' (Ranunculaceae) in a karst spring in central Europe |journal=Journal of Cave and Karst Studies: The National Speleological Society Bulletin |volume=73 |pages=158–161 |doi=10.4311/jcks20101sc0165|doi-broken-date=12 July 2025 }}</ref> and old mineral workings and canals in England.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Stewart |first1=A. |last2=Pearman |first2=D.A. |last3=Preston |first3=C.D. |title=Scarce Plants in Britain |date=1994 |publisher=Joint Nature Conservation Committee |location=Peterborough}}</ref> It favours the boundary between freshwater and fully saline conditions.

It is largely self-pollinated, and produces good seed, but it can also spread by fragments rooting on bare mud, thus colonising large areas very quickly, but it is unable to survive competition with dense emergent species such as ''[[Bolboschoenus maritimus]]''.

There are no insects recorded on brackish water-crowfoot specifically<ref>{{Cite web |title=Plant Parasites of Europe – leafminers, galls and fungi |url=https://bladmineerders.nl/ |access-date=2024-03-09 |website=bladmineerders.nl}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=BRC - Database of Insects and their Food Plants |url=https://dbif.brc.ac.uk/ |access-date=2024-03-09 |website=dbif.brc.ac.uk}}</ref> but various species feed on ''Ranunculus'' generally and can be found producing leaf mines and other damage to plants.
[[File:Ranunculus baudotii leaf mines.jpg|thumb|Insect damage to the leaves]]

==Distribution and status==
Brackish water-crowfoot occurs throughout Europe, extending just as far as North Africa and westernmost Asia, but it is absent or extinct in some inland regions and countries, such as Switzerland.<ref name=gbif>{{Cite web |title=Ranunculus baudotii Godr. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/3923698 |access-date=2024-03-09 |website=www.gbif.org |language=en}}</ref><ref name=powo>{{Cite web |title=Ranunculus baudotii Godr. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:712287-1 |access-date=2024-03-09 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref> Its threat status globally has been assessed as LC (Least Concern).<ref>{{Cite web |title=''Ranunculus peltatus'' subsp. ''baudotii'' (Godr.) Meikle ex C.D.K.Cook |url=https://eunis.eea.europa.eu/species/195465 |access-date=1 March 2024 |website=European Nature Information System}}</ref>

It is usually considered an [[axiophyte]], or plant of conservation importance, wherever it grows.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland |title=Axiophytes |url=https://bsbi.org/axiophytes}}</ref>

==Uses and in culture==
Members of the Ranunculaceae contain an irritating glycoside, ranunculin, from which the volatile substance [[protoanemonin]] is formed. Animals tend to avoid eating them because the taste is acrid, unless they are dried in hay or sprayed with herbicide.<ref name=poison>{{cite book |last1=Cooper |first1=M.R. |last2=Johnson |first2=A.W. |last3=Dauncey |first3=E.A. |title=Poisonous Plants and Fungi |date=2003 |publisher=The Stationery Office |location=London |isbn=0-11-702861-4}}</ref>
